Recently, Nvidia plunged by double digits at one point, dragging the entire tech sector down with it. But the market started recovering fairly quickly. Nvidia regained most of its losses, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq also stabilized.

Now, here's the big question. Why didn't crypto bounce back alongside the stock market? Instead, it kept falling, with Bitcoin eventually dropping to around $68,000.

Here's the hypothesis.

Recently, Binance was hacked, resulting in losses of approximately $6.3 billion. The exchange said it would fully reimburse the losses using its own funds. And we know for a fact that 7,500 BTC, worth approximately $580 million, were withdrawn from Binance's insurance fund afterward. Where exactly those coins went and whether they were sold on the market remains publicly unknown.

But it's entirely possible that Binance has been selling some of its own crypto holdings over the past few days to raise liquidity and cover the massive shortfall caused by the hack. And the panic surrounding Nvidia may have simply created the perfect backdrop for those sales to go largely unnoticed amid a broader market sell-off.

And there's one very important detail here. On November 12, Binance announced that the recovery of assets following the hack was complete.

If hypothesis is even partially correct, Bitcoin's current decline may have less to do with investors suddenly losing faith in crypto and more to do with the emergence of a massive forced seller.

And forced sellers are different from sellers in a typical bear market in one important way. Sooner or later, they run out of assets to sell.

That's why the next few days will be particularly interesting. If the selling pressure really did come from Binance and most of the necessary selling is already behind us, crypto could soon reveal just how strong the underlying demand was beneath all this selling pressure.
